explainedBy: The 10,000-hour rule starts with a violin student walking the halls of a Berlin music academy.

storyboard.claim: The 10,000-hour rule must be discussed, starting at the Berlin music academy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A violin student walks through the academy practice rooms, a violin beside her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the Berlin study sequence after the setup line.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the famous rule in the violin academy where the data came from.

explainedBy: Same student: behind the soundproof doors she sits down to intense, repetitive violin practice.

storyboard.claim: Behind soundproof doors, students repeat intense violin practice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The violin student now seated with the violin, strained face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; she stops walking and sits to practice, face turns strained.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the rig cannot draw bowing; the violin and the strained seated pose carry 'practice'.

explainedBy: The faculty sorts the elite students into three groups: good, better and best.

storyboard.claim: The students were grouped by the faculty into good, better and best.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-bucket sorter: Good | Better | Best.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From one student to the three groups the study compared.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the study's structure: three ranked groups.

explainedBy: Each student keeps a diary logging her day against the clock in 15-minute slices.

storyboard.claim: Students keep exhausting diaries tracking their lives in 15-minute increments.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The violin student holds a diary page beside a clock, tired face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Back from the groups to one student, now holding her diary.
storyboard.addedInformation: The clock + diary show the time-logging method of the study.

explainedBy: The diary's key entry is solo practice: the student alone with her violin, the origin of the rule.

storyboard.claim: Most important was time practicing alone; this study is the origin point of the rule.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same student, seated alone, the violin returns beside her, diary still in hand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the clock gives way to the violin and she sits: the diary's key column is solo practice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the measured variable: solo practice time.

explainedBy: Malcolm Gladwell holds up his bestseller Outliers, the book that made the 10,000-hour rule famous.

storyboard.claim: The 10,000-hour rule was popularized by Malcolm Gladwell's bestseller Outliers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gladwell, smiling, holding his book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the study to the book that popularized it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Identifies who spread the rule and through what: a bestselling book.

explainedBy: Ericsson objects to Gladwell's book: the rule bends what his Berlin study actually found.

storyboard.claim: The rule is largely a myth that bends what Ericsson actually discovered.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gladwell still holding his book while Ericsson points at it, angry.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; Ericsson enters and points at the book in objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the conflict: the scientist rejecting the popular version of his work.

explainedBy: An ordinary man sits out the hours beside the clock and nothing magical happens to him.

storyboard.claim: 10,000 hours is not a magical threshold that unlocks mastery.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An ordinary man seated beside a clock, blank face: hours pass, no transformation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the book's claim to a person living it out.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the negation: time passing with no aura of mastery appearing.

explainedBy: Same man, same clock: clocking the hours has left him with nothing, so he slumps.

storyboard.claim: Merely clocking 10,000 hours guarantees nothing; Gladwell is a fantastic storyteller.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same man beside the clock, now slumped and sad.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; blank face turns sad, he slumps.
storyboard.addedInformation: The result of hours alone: no guaranteed gain.

explainedBy: Gladwell's star example: the young Beatles playing hour after hour on a Hamburg club stage.

storyboard.claim: Gladwell's famous example: the Beatles playing 10,000 hours in Hamburg clubs before fame.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A 1960 club rocker with his guitar, energetic on the club stage.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the general myth to its most famous example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the scene the example describes: a band performing in a club.

explainedBy: The romantic story meets the record: a biographer's notes count how many hours the band really played.

storyboard.claim: It's a romantic story, but Beatles biographer Mark Lewisohn crunched the historical numbers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same rocker on stage stops celebrating; a sheet of notes appears beside him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the celebration stops and the record (notes) appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the biographer is not in the cast; the notes stand for the counted record.

explainedBy: The Hamburg 10,000-hour story is rejected: the band played nowhere near 10,000 hours.

storyboard.claim: They played only about a thousand hours in Hamburg, nowhere near 10,000.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum from 0 to 10,000 hours with the marker far to the left.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the counting to the result of the count.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the size of the gap between the myth and the record.

explainedBy: Playing covers to a drunken crowd goes in the Performing bucket, not the Deliberate practice bucket.

storyboard.claim: Playing cover songs to a crowd is performing, not deliberate, error-correcting practice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-bucket sorter: Performing | Deliberate practice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the number of hours to the kind of hours.
storyboard.addedInformation: States Ericsson's crux: the hours were the wrong kind.

explainedBy: The performer on stage plays to get through the song for the crowd, not to fix his weak chords.

storyboard.claim: Performing is the opposite of deliberate practice: the goal is to get through the song successfully.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The club rocker on stage, playing it up for the crowd.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Back from the sorter to the performer it describes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows performing's goal: a smooth show, not fixing weak spots.

explainedBy: The performer keeps smiling and hides his mistakes behind a show face.

storyboard.claim: Performers rely on what they know, avoid weaknesses and mask their mistakes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same rocker on stage, stops celebrating; a mask appears beside his smiling face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the celebration stops and the mask appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask shows the hidden-mistake side of performing.

explainedBy: Deliberate practice is the opposite: a learner examines his own mistakes under a magnifier.

storyboard.claim: Deliberate practice strips away performance and spotlights only your mistakes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An ordinary learner holding a magnifier up close, worried face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrast to the masking performer: now the mistakes are examined, not hidden.
storyboard.addedInformation: The magnifier shows scrutiny of one's own errors.

explainedBy: The host plays devil's advocate, holding up Ericsson's own Berlin numbers.

storyboard.claim: Playing devil's advocate: go back to Ericsson's own Berlin data.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host holding a page of data with a challenging smirk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the argument to the counter-argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: host commentary; the held data page marks the turn to the numbers.

explainedBy: The best students' 7,400 solo hours by age 18 project out to 10,000 hours by about 20.

storyboard.claim: The best students averaged 7,400 hours by 18, projecting to 10,000 by about 20.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: 7,400 hours -> 10,000 hours.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the host to the numbers themselves.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the projection the devil's advocate leans on.

explainedBy: The question puts Gladwell and his book back on screen next to the clock: maybe huge time really is required.

storyboard.claim: Isn't Gladwell right that massive amounts of time are required?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Gladwell holding his book, pleased, beside a clock.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the numbers back to Gladwell's claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties Gladwell's rule to the amount of time.

explainedBy: Same Gladwell: he got the spirit of hard work right, but the answer turns with a 'but'.

storyboard.claim: Gladwell captured the spirit of hard work, but...
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same Gladwell with book and clock; the smile turns to a knowing smirk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; happy turns to smirk as the concession comes.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the concession is carried mostly by the text.

explainedBy: Ericsson corrects Gladwell: 10,000 was only the average of one group, distorted into a catchy rule.

storyboard.claim: Gladwell distorted the science; 10,000 was just the average of that specific group.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Ericsson points while Gladwell, startled, listens.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Gladwell alone to Ericsson correcting him.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who corrects whom.

explainedBy: The elite students split: half had not reached 10,000 hours, some had gone well past it.

storyboard.claim: Half the elite students hadn't reached 10,000 hours and some had gone well past.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-bucket sorter: Not yet 10,000 | Well past it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the average to the spread behind it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the number was no threshold: students fell on both sides.

explainedBy: At 20, the violin student is promising but not a master, with ten more years of work ahead.

storyboard.claim: At 20 the students were not global masters but promising students with a decade of work ahead.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The violin student seated with her violin, serious face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Back to the student the numbers describe.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the student is still a student, not a finished master.

explainedBy: Competition winners around 30 have logged 20,000 to 25,000 hours, far past 10,000.

storyboard.claim: International competition winners are around 30 with 20,000-25,000 hours of practice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: 10,000 hours -> 20,000+ hours.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the promising student to where real masters are.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows mastery lies far beyond the rule's number.

explainedBy: The host dismisses the number 10,000 itself as arbitrary.

storyboard.claim: So the number 10,000 was completely arbitrary.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The host speaking, the number struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the number argument.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike labels the rejection of the number; commentary beat.

explainedBy: An office worker sits at his desk punching the clock, believing hours alone will make him CEO.

storyboard.claim: The danger: people think punching the clock at a desk job for 10,000 hours makes them a CEO.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An office worker seated at his desk beside a clock, blank face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the science to the everyday misuse of the rule.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the desk-job version of 'just put in the hours'.

explainedBy: Same worker, same clock: years in the comfort zone leave him a permanent amateur, slumped at his desk.

storyboard.claim: Hours in your comfort zone make you a permanent, deeply entrenched amateur.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same worker beside the clock, now slumped and sad.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; blank turns sad and he slumps: the result of the hours.
storyboard.addedInformation: The result: experience without growth.

explainedBy: What counts is sorted into two: the quality of the struggle, not the quantity of time.

storyboard.claim: It is about the quality of the struggle, not the quantity of time; comfort is where improvement stops.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-bucket sorter: Quality of the struggle | Quantity of the time.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the slumped worker to the principle.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the lesson as a contrast of two measures.

explainedBy: The lessons now move to the ordinary listener walking into his everyday job, briefcase in hand.

storyboard.claim: We need to apply these elite lessons to the listener's everyday professional life.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An ordinary worker walking in with a briefcase.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From elite performers to the ordinary listener.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the target of the next section: an everyday professional.

explainedBy: Young Franklin with a book, about to teach himself to write.

storyboard.claim: Most listeners aren't violinists or gymnasts; look at young Franklin, this time not playing chess.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The teenage apprentice Franklin walks into a room of books.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the listener to a historical everyday learner.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the case study; chess is deliberately not shown.

explainedBy: Wanting to be a writer, young Franklin picks up a copy of the Spectator magazine.

storyboard.claim: He wants to become a world-class writer and sits with a copy of The Spectator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same Franklin picks up a magazine.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; he stops and takes up the magazine.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows his practice material: a model text.

explainedBy: Franklin hides the magazine and labors to rewrite the essay from his cryptic notes.

storyboard.claim: He makes cryptic notes, hides the magazine, and days later labors to rewrite the essay from them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Franklin holding his notes, straining.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The magazine is put away; now he works from notes only.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the method's core step: rebuilding the essay from notes.

explainedBy: Same Franklin, seated with only his notes, rebuilds the original's vocabulary, logic and rhythm from memory.

storyboard.claim: He rewrites from memory, trying to match the vocabulary, logic and rhythm of the original.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same Franklin, now seated, still holding only his notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; he sits down to the work.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: 'from memory' is carried by the absence of the magazine and the text.

callout.text: his own failures in red ink

explainedBy: Franklin compares his version with the original and marks his own failures in red ink.

storyboard.claim: He compares them side by side, marks his failures in red ink, and does it again.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same Franklin with his notes; a page covered in red corrections appears.
storyboard.onScreenText: his own failures in red ink
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the red-ink page appears: the feedback step.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the feedback he built for himself.

explainedBy: The professional with a briefcase: years on a job without scores or coaching can be a trap.

storyboard.claim: Self-directed practice matters because professional experience is often a trap without scores or coaching.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The office worker slumped and worried at his job.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From Franklin's self-made feedback to the worker who has none.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the person caught in the trap.

explainedBy: Same worker: without feedback his years just repeat the same mistakes.

storyboard.claim: Years on the job may entrench bad habits; you must manufacture your own feedback like Franklin.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same worker, worry turns to sadness.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; worried turns sad.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the face change carries the cost; 'feedback loops' are text only.

explainedBy: A radiologist examines a mammogram scan, the subject of a 2004 study.

storyboard.claim: A 2004 study looked at radiologists analyzing mammograms to detect breast cancer.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A radiologist in a hospital studying a scan with a magnifier.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the office to a hospital case study.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who was studied and what they do.

noVisual: A correlation (or its absence) between two measures has no diagram type; years are shown by the clock and the finding by the callout.
explainedBy: Same radiologist beside the clock of his years: those years do not make his diagnoses more accurate.

storyboard.claim: There was zero correlation between radiologists' years of experience and their diagnostic accuracy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same radiologist with a clock (years) appearing, surprised face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same stage; the clock of experience appears and the face turns surprised.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the finding itself is text-carried.
